==Problem==
Joy has <math>30</math> thin rods, one each of every integer length from <math>1</math> cm through <math>30</math> cm. She places the rods with lengths <math>3</math> cm, <math>7</math> cm, and <math>15</math> cm on a table. She then wants to choose a fourth rod that she can put with these three to form a quadrilateral with positive area. How many of the remaining rods can she choose as the fourth rod?

<math>\textbf{(A)}\ 16\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 17\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 18\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 19\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 20</math>

==Solution 1==
The triangle inequality generalizes to all polygons, so <imath>x < 3+7+15</imath> and <imath>15<x+3+7</imath> yields <imath>5<x<25</imath>. Now, we know that there are <imath>19</imath> numbers between <imath>5</imath> and <imath>25</imath> exclusive, but we must subtract <imath>2</imath> to account for the 2 lengths already used that are between those numbers, which gives <imath>19-2=\boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ 17}</imath>

==Solution 2 (Auxiliary Line)==
If you do not know the fact that the Triangle Inequality applies to all polygons, you can can solve it completely using the standard triangle inequality that you already know by simply splitting the quadrilateral into two triangles.  Let the four sides of our quadrilateral be <imath>3</imath>, <imath>7</imath>, <imath>15</imath>, and <imath>x</imath>. Draw an auxiliary diagonal line <imath>y</imath> that splits the shape into a small triangle with sides <imath>3</imath>, <imath>7</imath>, and <imath>y</imath>, and a larger triangle with sides <imath>15</imath>, <imath>x</imath>, and <imath>y</imath>.

Applying the standard triangle inequality to the first triangle with sides <imath>3</imath>, <imath>7</imath>, and <imath>y</imath> gives us <imath>7 - 3 < y < 7 + 3</imath>, which simplifies to <imath>4 < y < 10</imath>. Note that <imath>y</imath> is an imaginary line segment slicing through continuous space, meaning it can be any real decimal value in this interval and does not need to be strictly integers.

Next, we apply the triangle inequality to the second triangle with sides <imath>15</imath>, <imath>x</imath>, and <imath>y</imath> to determine the boundaries of <imath>x</imath>. For the upper bound, the unknown side must satisfy <imath>x < 15 + y</imath>. As <imath>y</imath> maximizes and approaches but never reaches <imath>10</imath>, the absolute upper bound approaches <imath>15 + 10 = 25</imath>, meaning <imath>x < 25</imath>. For the lower bound, the side of length <imath>15</imath> must satisfy <imath>15 < x + y</imath>, which reshapes into <imath>x > 15 - y</imath>. To minimize <imath>x</imath>, we subtract the maximum possible upper limit of <imath>y</imath> (which approaches <imath>10</imath>), giving <imath>x > 15 - 10 = 5</imath>.

Combining both boundaries gives us the range <imath>5 < x < 25</imath>. Since <imath>x</imath> must be an integer, the valid values are <imath>6</imath> through <imath>24</imath> inclusive. The total count of integers in this pool is <imath>24 - 6 + 1 = 19</imath>. However, the question states that the rods must be chosen from the remaining pile. The rods of length <imath>7\text{ cm}</imath> and <imath>15\text{ cm}</imath> are already placed on the table to build the other sides of the quadrilateral, so they are unavailable to be chosen again. Subtracting these <imath>2</imath> unavailable choices yields our final total of <imath>19 - 2 = \boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ 17}</imath>.
